findings.text: The first paragraph does its job. A newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, all before the first heading.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The title is about a different project, firstmate. Someone who came to Athena's own site will not see from the title that this is Athena's home page. It takes three paragraphs to learn that the page is a demo study.

The first section after the navigation is an error message. It sits where the pitch promised proof: models, verdict and cost. A newcomer sees the main selling point fail to appear on the project's own page.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: The header sends a first-time visitor to an owner-only page with no explanation. A newcomer has no proposals, so the link raises a question instead of guiding them.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision.

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: they list prerequisites, give the clone and setup commands, and show a first command with what it does. The header also links straight to this section.
findings.source: Next steps: "git 2.40 or later; a C linker (cc) ...; curl ...; Claude Code, or npm to install it." / "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" / "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page promises two different models but never says which second model is used. It also never mentions the accounts, API keys or spending each model needs. A newcomer cannot judge the setup cost or the cost of running a request.
findings.source: "has one AI model do the work and a different one check it" vs prerequisites listing only "Claude Code, or npm to install it"

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense study of firstmate's internals: captain, yolo, places-held, exit 75, pending-close records. A newcomer to Athena does not need any of this to decide whether to try Athena. The expert toggle hides only Counters and Transitions.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Transitions" (t1–t12), "Glossary", "Claims and sources" (c1–c45)

findings.text: Every statement is traced to a claim, and every claim to specific lines in firstmate's files at a fixed commit. This shows Athena's claim of traceability in action, and the "Check a statement" step tells the reader how to verify it.
findings.source: Each statement ends with claim links, e.g. "[c1]", and each claim links to "AGENTS.md:206-206" at the pinned commit

findings.text: The page is honest about gaps, but several glossary entries define nothing. A newcomer meets terms that stay unexplained.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a durable record." / "The firstmate source does not define a heartbeat." / "in scope ... this page gives no test for it"

findings.text: The page states openly that it only read firstmate's code and ran none of it. That is good for trust, but with the failed job record it means the page never shows Athena actually running.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
